newsitem.title: USA: Scientist who inspired Hubble telescope dies.
newsitem.headline: Scientist who inspired Hubble telescope dies.

text.p: Lyman Spitzer, architect of the Hubble space telescope and creator of experiments to generate fusion power, died at his home in Princeton on Monday, Princeton University officials said on Wednesday. He was 82.

His death occurred three days before the mothballing of the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, for budgetary reasons. It was a leader in the worldwide search to harness the energy released by the fusion of hydrogen atoms -- the same process that gives stars their immense energy.

Astrophysics was Dr. Spitzer's core speciality, and he chaired the university's department of astrophysics and directed the Princeton Observatory until 1979. But he never retired, reviewing data from the Hubble telescope until shortly before he died.

That project originated in a 1946 proposal by Spitzer, more than a decade before the launch of the Soviet Sputnik satellites. His concept was tested first with a telescope lifted 20 miles (32 km) up by balloons in 1957 and led to the 1972 launch of the Copernicus ultraviolet satellite.
Spitzer's tireless advocacy kept the project alive for another 33 years.
He was a Yale undergraduate and attended Cambridge University before earning advanced degrees at Princeton in 1937.
Upon returning to Princeton in 1947, he urged that thermonuclear fusion be studied as an alternative to fission power.

The plasma physics lab, with its large doughnut shaped reactor, surrounded by magnets to control the superheated plasma, opened in 1956. But in recent years, its budget was cut to the point that its board had to end its operations, effective on Thursday.

Spitzer also was influential in developing the theory of stellar dynamics -- the idea that stars lose and regain energy through a cyclical lifetime -- and in the study of interstellar matter, the dust and gases that form magnetic fields between stars.
